newsitem.title: KENYA: MINOR DELAYS AT NAIROBI AIRPORT - FREIGHT SOURCES.
newsitem.headline: MINOR DELAYS AT NAIROBI AIRPORT - FREIGHT SOURCES.

text.p: Freight forwarders and foreign airlines said on Thursday afternoon they only were facing minor delays at Nairobi airport after air traffic controllers ended a five-day go-slow.
The action ended after negotiations with the government earlier on Thursday but industry sources said major delays still remained in the south.

"The situation is back to normal, both air traffic controllers and meteorological staff are back working and there are only minor delays at Nairobi airport," an official with the International Air Transport Association(IATA) here told Reuters.
An official from a major airline said the go-slow at Mombasa's airport was continuing, however.

Airlines and forwarders also said they did not expect a national strike called for Friday would have a major impact on air operations. The strike by an opposition-backed alliance of groups seeking constitutional reforms has been declared illegal by the government.

Both air cargo and passengers had been facing major delays on flights out of Kenya since the go-slow was launched last Friday midnight, crippling business at both Nairobi and Mombasa international airports. The latter is Kenya's second city and centre of its tourism industry.
"The situation is much better today, let's hope things work out," said an official with Dutch-owned freight forwarder Flower Wings.
British Airways Plc said it expected to have its passenger Boeing 747 would leave on schedule Thursday evening at 1925 GMT.

"We are hoping that none of our flights are delayed, but we expect the flight to depart on schedule, the situation is back to normal," Tony Nothman, regional cargo manager for British Airways, told Reuters.

British Airways operate daily passenger flights between Nairobi and London in addition to two weekly freighters, normally a Douglas DC-8 or Boeing-707 carrying up to 38 tonnes, every Tuesday and Saturday, Nothman said.
He said most cargo on BA's two last freight flights had been affected by the go-slow. It mostly consisted of perishable products which had been delayed for "several hours".
But Nothman could not say whether BA was expecting any losses from the delays faced this week, saying only: "We will have to wait and see if we do get any claims from any of our customers."
